Calculate prevalence, confidence intervals, significance tests and trend

Source: R/prevalence.R
calc_prevalence.Rd

Calculates survey-weighted prevalence estimates and confidence intervals for a binary outcome over single years, rolling multi-year periods or user-defined groups of years, and (optionally) tests whether the prevalence differs significantly between periods or between subgroups, and whether there is a linear trend over time. Different analysis populations can be specified for different outcomes through the denominator variable.

Usage

calc_prevalence(
  data,
  denominator,
  year_var,
  outcome_var,
  weight_var = NULL,
  psu = NULL,
  strata = NULL,
  by = NULL,
  rolling_year = 1,
  periods = NULL,
  ci_level = 0.95,
  digits = 1,
  test = TRUE,
  compare_var = "rolling_period",
  compare_to = "first",
  p_adjust = "none",
  trend = TRUE
)

Arguments

data

A data frame or data.table containing the survey data.

denominator

Character string giving the name of a binary denominator/eligibility variable. Observations with denominator == 1 are included in the analysis population; observations with denominator == 0 are excluded. The denominator variable therefore defines the population to which the prevalence estimate applies.

year_var

Character string giving the name of the variable containing the calendar year (whole numbers).

outcome_var

Character string giving the name of the binary outcome variable. The outcome must be coded as 0 and 1, where 1 indicates the outcome of interest.

weight_var

Optional character string giving the name of the survey weight variable. If NULL, an unweighted prevalence is calculated. Default is NULL.

psu

Optional character string giving the name of the primary sampling unit (PSU) variable. If NULL (the default), every observation is treated as its own sampling unit.

strata

Optional character string giving the name of the survey stratum variable. If NULL (the default), no stratification is specified.

by

Optional character vector giving the names of variables defining subgroups for which prevalence should be calculated. If NULL, estimates are calculated for the entire analysis population within each period.

rolling_year

Positive integer specifying the number of calendar years included in each rolling period. The default is 1, i.e. prevalence is calculated separately for each year. Use e.g. rolling_year = 3 for three-year rolling periods. Ignored (with a warning if it is not 1) when periods is supplied.

periods

Optional named list defining your own periods, instead of rolling periods. Each element is a vector of calendar years and the element name is the label used for that period in the output, e.g. list("2013-2015" = 2013:2015, "2016-2025" = 2016:2025). The periods are kept in the order you give them, which matters for compare_to = "first", compare_to = "previous" and the trend. Periods may have different lengths and may overlap. If NULL (the default), rolling periods defined by rolling_year are used. No recoding of the year variable is needed.

ci_level

Numeric value between 0 and 1 specifying the confidence level for the confidence intervals. The default is 0.95. The significance level used in the tests is alpha = 1 - ci_level.

digits

Number of digits used when rounding the results (percentages and percentage-point differences). Default is 1. P-values are not rounded.

test

Logical. If TRUE (the default), significance tests between periods or subgroups are calculated and returned in $tests. If FALSE, $tests is NULL.

compare_var

Character string giving the dimension along which prevalence is compared. Either "rolling_period" (the default; compare periods, i.e. change over time) or one of the variables in by (compare subgroups). Comparisons are always made within the levels of all other variables in by. For example, with by = c("gender", "region") and compare_var = "gender", men and women are compared within each region and period. (The period variable is always called rolling_period in the output, also when you define the periods with periods.)

compare_to

Defines the reference for the comparisons. One of:

  • "first" (the default): every level is compared with the first level (e.g. the earliest period).

  • "previous": every level is compared with the level immediately before it (e.g. the previous period).

  • A character string giving a specific level of compare_var (e.g. "2013-2015", a label from periods, or "Female"): every other level is compared with that level.

p_adjust

Method for adjusting p-values for multiple comparisons. Any of stats::p.adjust.methods, e.g. "none" (the default), "holm", "bonferroni" or "BH". The adjustment is applied across all comparisons in $tests (and separately across the trend tests in $trend).

trend

Logical. If TRUE (the default), a linear trend test over the periods is calculated and returned in $trend, together with the fitted trend line and its confidence interval in $fitted. The trend is estimated separately for each combination of the by variables. At least three periods are required, so use trend = FALSE when you only define two periods with periods.

Value

A named list with four elements:

estimates

A data.table with one row per period (and per combination of the by variables) and the columns rolling_period, the by variables, prevalence (percent), se (percentage points), ci_lower, ci_upper (percent) and n (unweighted number of observations).

tests

A data.table with one row per comparison (or NULL if test = FALSE or there is nothing to compare). Columns: the variables held fixed in the comparison (if any), reference and compared (the levels being compared), prev_ref and prev_cmp (prevalence in percent), diff (prev_cmp - prev_ref in percentage points), diff_se, diff_ci_lower, diff_ci_upper, z, p_value, p_adjusted and significant (TRUE if p_adjusted < 1 - ci_level).

trend

A data.table with one row per combination of the by variables (or NULL if trend = FALSE or fewer than three periods are available). Columns: the by variables, first_period, last_period, n_periods, slope (average change in percentage points per year), slope_se, slope_ci_lower, slope_ci_upper, z, p_value, p_adjusted, significant and direction ("increasing", "decreasing" or "no significant trend").

fitted

A data.table with the fitted trend line, one row per period (and per combination of the by variables), or NULL if trend = FALSE or no trend could be estimated. Columns: the by variables, rolling_period, time (the mean year of the period, used as the x value), prevalence (the observed estimate, percent), fitted (the value on the trend line, percent) and lwr, upr (the confidence interval for the fitted line, percent).

Details

Analysis population. The denominator argument defines the analysis population for the selected outcome. Only observations with denominator == 1 are used. The restriction is applied before missing outcomes are removed, periods are constructed and the survey design is created, so the denominator defines the population from which both the prevalence and its variance are estimated. Missing values in denominator cause an error. Observations with missing outcome_var are removed.

Survey design. The design is constructed with survey::svydesign() (with nest = TRUE). Estimates and variances come from survey::svyby() and survey::svymean(). When PSU and/or strata information are available they should be supplied so that the variance estimator accounts for the complex sampling design.

Rolling periods. With rolling_year = 3, the estimate for 2022 uses observations from 2020 through 2022. Only periods in which all calendar years are present in the data are created. Periods overlap, so one observation can contribute to several periods.

Custom periods. With periods you choose the groups of years yourself, for example to compare a baseline period with all later years. All observations from the listed years are pooled into one estimate for that period. Years listed in periods that are not in the (eligible) data give a warning; a period without any observations gives an error. Because the pooled estimate for a long period is a weighted average over its years, it is only comparable with another period if the survey weights are comparable across the years.

Significance tests. For each comparison the difference in prevalence between two estimates, \(\hat{p}_2 - \hat{p}_1\), is tested with a Wald z-test: $$ z = \frac{\hat{p}_2 - \hat{p}_1}{\sqrt{V(\hat{p}_1) + V(\hat{p}_2) - 2\,\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{p}_1, \hat{p}_2)}}. $$ The covariance is taken from the survey design (via svyby(..., covmat = TRUE)). This matters for overlapping periods (rolling periods or overlapping periods), because they share observations and their estimates are therefore correlated; ignoring the covariance would give wrong standard errors. Each observation is kept as one sampling unit (or the PSU, if supplied) across all periods it appears in, which is what allows the covariance to be estimated. Confidence intervals for the differences use the same normal approximation and the level given by ci_level. The normal approximation is also what stats::confint() uses for svyby objects, so the tests and the confidence intervals in $estimates are consistent.

Trend test. The trend is the slope of a straight line fitted to the prevalence estimates against the midpoint year of each period (the mean of the years in the period), so slope is the average change in percentage points per year. The line is fitted by generalized least squares using the full covariance matrix of the estimates from the survey design, which accounts for the overlap between periods (ordinary regression on overlapping estimates would treat them as independent and give far too small standard errors). The slope is tested with a Wald z-test. This is a test of a linear trend; a non-linear development (e.g. flat and then rising) can still give a significant slope, so inspect the estimates as well. The trend is a separate question from the pairwise comparisons controlled by compare_var/compare_to.

Fitted trend line. $fitted contains the value of the same GLS line at each period, \(\hat{y}_t = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 t\), with a confidence interval \(\hat{y}_t \pm z \cdot SE(\hat{y}_t)\), where \(SE(\hat{y}_t)\) comes from the covariance matrix of the estimated coefficients. This is the confidence interval for the line (the average development), in the same way as predict(lm(...), interval = "confidence"); it is not a prediction interval for a single new estimate and it is not the same as the confidence interval of the observed prevalence in $estimates. Because the line is not restricted, lwr and upr can fall below 0 or above 100 for very low or very high prevalence. The fitted values use exactly the same fit as the slope in $trend, so the plotted line and the reported slope always agree. Unlike lm(), the fit uses the survey covariance matrix, so the line is not the same as an ordinary least-squares line through the period estimates.

Interpretation. significant = TRUE means that the difference is statistically significant at level 1 - ci_level after the chosen multiple-comparison adjustment. A statistically significant difference is not necessarily a large or important one; consider the size of diff and its confidence interval. When many comparisons are made, consider using p_adjust.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# Annual prevalence, change over time compared with the first year
res <- calc_prevalence(
  data = dt,
  denominator = "eligible",
  year_var = "year",
  outcome_var = "outcome",
  weight_var = "weight",
  rolling_year = 1
)
res$estimates
res$tests
res$trend
res$fitted   # fitted trend line with confidence interval, e.g. for plotting

# Three-year rolling prevalence with PSU and strata, each period
# compared with the previous one, Holm-adjusted p-values
calc_prevalence(
  data = dt,
  denominator = "eligible",
  year_var = "year",
  outcome_var = "outcome",
  weight_var = "weight",
  psu = "psu",
  strata = "stratum",
  rolling_year = 3,
  compare_to = "previous",
  p_adjust = "holm"
)

# Custom periods: 2013-2015 compared with 2016-2025.
# No new year column is needed. Only two periods, so no trend.
calc_prevalence(
  data = dt,
  denominator = "eligible",
  year_var = "year",
  outcome_var = "outcome",
  weight_var = "weight",
  periods = list(
    "2013-2015" = 2013:2015,
    "2016-2025" = 2016:2025
  ),
  trend = FALSE
)

# Custom periods by gender: three periods, each compared with the
# baseline period, with a trend over the three periods
calc_prevalence(
  data = dt,
  denominator = "eligible",
  year_var = "year",
  outcome_var = "outcome",
  weight_var = "weight",
  by = "gender",
  periods = list(
    "2013-2016" = 2013:2016,
    "2017-2020" = 2017:2020,
    "2021-2025" = 2021:2025
  ),
  compare_to = "2013-2016"
)

# Compare genders within each rolling period
calc_prevalence(
  data = dt,
  denominator = "eligible",
  year_var = "year",
  outcome_var = "outcome",
  weight_var = "weight",
  psu = "psu",
  strata = "stratum",
  by = c("region", "gender"),
  rolling_year = 3,
  compare_var = "gender",
  compare_to = "Male"
)

# Estimates only, no tests and no trend
calc_prevalence(
  data = dt, denominator = "eligible", year_var = "year",
  outcome_var = "outcome", weight_var = "weight",
  test = FALSE, trend = FALSE
)$estimates
} # }
